latin.378: GAR. Et cum lapsu suo Adam non modo exciderit justitia sua, sed in omnigenas calamitates incidere commeruerit; si quis agnoscat ad justitiam amittendam nihil opus fuisse judiciaria actione, fatebitur saltem ad poenas subeundas eam intervenire oportuisse: hoc est enim praecipue illud morte morieris.
latin.379: PLAC. Id equidem fateor: Extat enim illa sententia Gen. 3. Sed quid inde sequitur? Potestne ostendere vir doctus in Scriptura judiciariam aliquam Dei sententiam, qua fuerit Adamus spoliatus justitia? Et tamen non assentior viro docto poenas sententia lata Gen. 3. 16. 17. Evae & Adamo irrogatas, eas fuisse, quas lex praecipue comminabatur verbis morte morieris. Id enim pugnat cum Christi satisfactione, & fidelium propter eam justificatione plena & perfecta.
latin.380: GAR. Adde quod fieri poterat, ut Adam peccando amitteret justitiam meritorie, & tamen ex Dei benignitate eam conservaret, quomodo nimirum in statu Gratiae, peccando, meritorie amittimus Gratiam, fidem, charitatem, nec tamen actu ab eis excidimus, quia Dei gratia superabundat, Roman. 5. 20.
latin.381: PLAC. Primum quid est amittere justitiam meritorie, nisi mereri non justificari a judice, sed condemnari? Nam mereri, ut pro poena judex ab eo auferat justitiae habitum, est mereri ut judex tollat quod non est, & faciat id quod cum justitia legislatoris & judicis pugnare videtur. Tenetur enim potius judex conservare justitiam, quam destruere, & ab eo qui ea praeditus est, tollere. Nec enim eum decet eos, quos judicat, facere injustos & peccatores. Comparatio quam instituit inter fideles in statu gratiae, & Adamum in statu naturae, quam non sit apposita, nemo, opinor, non videt. Opponuntur enim inter se, tantum abest ut sint similes, status naturae lapsae, & status gratiae. Justitia Adami erat donum naturale, justitia nobis inhaerens est donum supernaturale.
latin.382: Status naturae erat mutabilis, cum status gratiae sit incorruptibilis. Principium enim justitiae, seu sanctitatis nobis inherentis, non est mutabilis natura; sed immutabilis Spiritus Sanctus, unio cum Christo indissolubilis, propositum secundum electionem firmum; itaque peccatum est a vetere homine, a carne, justitia est a novo homine, a Spiritu: non igitur mirum videri debet, si peccata quaedam non privent nos habitu justitiae: quandoquidem illius habitus radices valde distant a radicibus peccati, & vita nostra spiritualis est aeterna, & Gratia comparata est ad medendum peccato. Sed quid erat in Adamo, quod impediret, quominus actualis eius a Deo Apostasia expelleret habitualem obedientiam seu justitiam? Mutato enim, ut dixi, fine ultimo, moralia mutari omnia necesse est. Id quod ipsum etiam cernere est, cum quis corde vel e falsa religione transit ad veram, vel e vera ad falsam. Quanta enim consequi solet studiorum & vivendi rationis commutatio?
latin.383: Praeterea privato Aulico titulis, dignitatibus & fundis, iisdem privantur eius filii, & nocet iis patris infidelitas. Confiteor etiam lapsum Adami nobis obfuisse & quidem vehementer, & quam ille fuit privatus justitia & rectitudine tam iisdem nos privatos ab eo gigni. Sed putasne crimen Aulici imputari a judice eius filiis nascituris & nepotibus?

pass_a.378: GAR grants for argument that losing justice needed no judicial act, yet says that by his fall Adam not only dropped justice but deserved to fall into calamities of every kind—so if one grants no judicial action for losing justice, one must at least confess that for undergoing penalties a judicial action ought to have intervened. That, he says, is chiefly what dying you shall die means.
pass_a.379: Placeus grants the Gen. 3 sentence stands, but asks what follows. Can GAR show any Scripture judicial sentence by which Adam was stripped of justice? He will not grant that the Gen. 3:16–17 penalties on Eve and Adam were what the law chiefly threatened by dying you shall die—that fights Christ's satisfaction and the faithful's full justification on account of it.
pass_a.380: GAR adds: Adam might lose justice meritoriously by sinning and yet keep it by God's benignity—as in the state of grace we meritoriously lose grace, faith, and charity by sinning yet do not actually fall from them, because grace superabounds (Rom. 5:20).
pass_a.381: Placeus: to lose justice meritoriously is only to deserve not to be justified by the judge but to be condemned. To deserve that a judge as punishment strip the habit of justice is to deserve that he take away what is not and do what fights a lawgiver's and judge's justice—he is bound rather to conserve justice than destroy it or take it from the endowed, and it does not become him to make those he judges into unjust sinners. Comparing the faithful in grace with Adam in nature is inapt: fallen nature and the state of grace are opposed, not alike. Adam's justice was a natural gift; the justice inhering in us is a supernatural gift.
pass_a.382: Nature's state was mutable; grace's is incorruptible. The principle of justice or holiness inhering in us is not mutable nature but the immutable Holy Spirit, indissoluble union with Christ, and a firm purpose according to election—so sin is from the old man and the flesh, justice from the new man and the Spirit. No wonder certain sins do not deprive us of the habit of justice: that habit's roots are far from sin's, our spiritual life is eternal, and Grace is fitted to heal sin. In Adam nothing hindered actual apostasy from God from expelling habitual obedience or justice—the last end being changed, all morals must change, as when the heart passes from false religion to true or true to false and studies and living change.
pass_a.383: Further: when the courtier loses titles, dignities, and estates, his sons lose them too, and the father's unfaithfulness harms them. Placeus grants Adam's fall harmed us vehemently—we are begotten deprived as he was of justice and rectitude. But does a judge impute the courtier's crime to sons yet unborn and to grandsons? Tip before GAR's Denique on parental crime descending.

378: GAR. And since by his fall Adam not only fell from his justice but deserved to fall into calamities of every kind; if anyone acknowledges that for losing justice there was no need of a judicial action, he will at least confess that for undergoing penalties it ought to have intervened: for that is chiefly what dying you shall die means.
379: PLAC. That I indeed confess: for that sentence in Gen. 3 stands. But what follows from it? Can the learned man show in Scripture any judicial sentence of God by which Adam was stripped of justice? And yet I do not assent to the learned man that the penalties inflicted on Eve and Adam by the sentence given in Gen. 3:16–17 were those which the law chiefly threatened by the words dying you shall die. For that fights with Christ's satisfaction, and with the full and perfect justification of the faithful on account of it.
380: GAR. Add that it could happen that Adam by sinning lost justice meritoriously, and yet by God's benignity conserved it—just as in the state of Grace, by sinning, we meritoriously lose Grace, faith, charity, and yet do not actually fall from them, because God's grace superabounds, Rom. 5:20.
381: PLAC. First, what is it to lose justice meritoriously, if not to deserve not to be justified by the judge, but to be condemned? For to deserve that as punishment the judge take from him the habit of justice is to deserve that the judge take away what is not, and do what seems to fight with the justice of the lawgiver and of the judge. For the judge is rather bound to conserve justice than to destroy it, and to take it from him who is endowed with it. Nor does it become him to make those whom he judges unjust and sinners. That the comparison he institutes between the faithful in the state of grace and Adam in the state of nature is not apt, no one, I think, fails to see. For they are opposed to each other—so far are they from being alike—the state of fallen nature and the state of grace. Adam's justice was a natural gift; the justice inhering in us is a supernatural gift.
382: The state of nature was mutable, whereas the state of grace is incorruptible. For the principle of the justice or holiness inhering in us is not mutable nature, but the immutable Holy Spirit, an indissoluble union with Christ, a firm purpose according to election; and so sin is from the old man, from the flesh, justice from the new man, from the Spirit: it ought not therefore seem strange if certain sins do not deprive us of the habit of justice—seeing that the roots of that habit are far distant from the roots of sin, and our spiritual life is eternal, and Grace is fitted to heal sin. But what was there in Adam that would hinder his actual apostasy from God from expelling habitual obedience or justice? For the last end being changed, as I said, all morals must of necessity be changed. Which itself is also seen when someone in heart passes either from a false religion to the true, or from the true to a false. How great a change of studies and of the way of living is accustomed to follow?
383: Besides, when the Courtier is deprived of titles, dignities, and estates, his sons are deprived of the same, and the father's unfaithfulness harms them. I also confess that Adam's fall harmed us, and indeed vehemently, and that as he was deprived of justice and rectitude, so we are begotten by him deprived of the same. But do you think the Courtier's crime is imputed by the judge to his sons yet to be born and to his grandsons?
